meta.title: Mathematics — the foundations of reasoning
meta.note: Explanations authored for Bucket Academy (original prose; equations and standard definitions are facts). Open sources only. Foundations-first DAG spanning logic & proof, sets and number systems, elementary and abstract algebra, linear algebra, calculus and analysis, probability and combinatorics, topology and metric spaces, differential equations, and a few frontier/foundational nodes (Gödel, computability, category theory).

atoms.title: Sets and functions
atoms.summary: A set is a collection of objects; a function is a rule assigning to each input exactly one output. These are the nouns and verbs of all modern mathematics.

depths.eli5: A set is a bag of things. A function is a machine: put one thing in, get exactly one thing out — never two, never none.
depths.core: Almost every mathematical object is built from sets, and almost every relationship between them is a function. The defining property is single-valuedness: each x in the domain X maps to one y in the codomain Y. Injective means no two inputs share an output; surjective means every output is hit; bijective means both, which is exactly when an inverse exists.
depths.deep: Functions compose, and composition is associative, which quietly makes 'sets and functions' a category — the ambient stage on which limits, groups, and spaces are later defined. Cardinality (size compared by bijection) already escapes intuition here: the integers and the rationals have the same cardinality, but the reals do not.

atoms.note: Distinguish the function f from its value f(x): one is the machine, the other is a single output.
atoms.art_prompt: two labeled bags of dots with single arrows leaving each left dot for exactly one right dot, none branching

quiz.prompt: What property must a relation between X and Y have to be a function, and what extra property makes it invertible?
quiz.answer: Each input maps to exactly one output (single-valued, total on X) to be a function; it is invertible exactly when it is bijective — both injective and surjective.

quiz.prompt: Is f(x) = x^2 from the reals to the reals injective? Surjective? How does restricting the codomain or domain change the answer?
quiz.answer: Not injective (x and -x collide) and not surjective onto all reals (negatives are never hit). Restrict the codomain to [0,∞) to make it surjective, and the domain to [0,∞) to make it injective; with both it becomes a bijection.

atoms.title: Limits and continuity
atoms.summary: A limit pins down what value a function approaches; continuity is when that approached value equals the actual value. The epsilon–delta game makes 'approaches' precise.

depths.eli5: If you can always get the output as close to a target as someone demands by making the input close enough to a point, that target is the limit. If the limit is just the value at the point, the function has no jumps there.
depths.core: The limit L is the number f(x) can be forced arbitrarily near (within any ε) by keeping x within some δ of a — without ever needing x = a. Continuity at a means the limit exists and equals f(a). This single definition tames the infinite: it lets us reason about 'getting close' using only finite inequalities.
depths.deep: The order of quantifiers is the whole subject: ε is chosen by an adversary first, δ is your response. Uniform continuity strengthens this by demanding one δ work for all a at once. Completeness of the reals is what guarantees the limits we expect actually exist — Cauchy sequences converge, and no points are 'missing'.

atoms.note: ε comes first, δ responds. Swap the order and you have defined uniform continuity instead.
atoms.art_prompt: a curve approaching a target height with shrinking horizontal and vertical tolerance bands nested around the point

quiz.prompt: In the epsilon–delta definition, who 'chooses' ε and who 'chooses' δ, and what does continuity at a add to the existence of the limit?
quiz.answer: The adversary fixes ε first; you must then produce a δ that works. Continuity at a additionally requires the limit to equal the function's actual value f(a).

quiz.prompt: Why is the function that is 0 on the rationals and 1 on the irrationals discontinuous at every point?
quiz.answer: Near any point both rationals and irrationals appear within any δ, so f takes both 0 and 1 arbitrarily close by; no single L can sit within ε < 1/2 of both, so the limit never exists.

atoms.title: Groups
atoms.summary: A group is a set with one associative operation that has an identity and inverses. It is the minimal axiom system for 'symmetry' and 'reversible composition'.

depths.eli5: A group is a set of moves you can do and undo, where doing two in a row is itself a move, and one 'do-nothing' move exists. Shuffling a deck or rotating a square both follow these rules.
depths.core: Four axioms — closure, associativity, an identity element e, and an inverse for every element — capture an astonishing range of structure: integers under addition, invertible matrices under multiplication, symmetries of any object. Abelian groups add commutativity. The power is that anything proven from the axioms holds for every group at once.
depths.deep: Groups act on sets, and the orbit–stabilizer theorem ties the size of an orbit to a subgroup index, turning counting problems into algebra. Lagrange's theorem (subgroup order divides group order) constrains structure before you know any specifics. The classification of finite simple groups — the 'periodic table' of symmetry — is one of mathematics' largest collective proofs.

atoms.note: Associativity is doing heavy lifting: it lets you write abc with no parentheses and is what fails for, e.g., the cross product.
atoms.art_prompt: a square with arrows showing its four rotational symmetries closing back on themselves as a cycle

quiz.prompt: Name the four group axioms.
quiz.answer: Closure under the operation, associativity, existence of an identity element, and existence of an inverse for every element.

quiz.prompt: Are the integers under multiplication a group? Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No — multiplication is associative with identity 1, but most integers (everything except ±1) lack a multiplicative inverse in the integers, so the inverse axiom fails.

atoms.title: The derivative
atoms.summary: The derivative is the best linear approximation to a function near a point — its instantaneous rate of change, and the slope of the tangent line.

depths.eli5: Zoom in on a smooth curve far enough and it looks like a straight line. The derivative is the slope of that line — how fast the output changes as you nudge the input.
depths.core: f'(a) is the limit of average rates of change f(a+h)/h as the window h shrinks to zero. Equivalently, it is the number m for which f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + mh with error vanishing faster than h. This 'local linearity' is why calculus works: hard nonlinear behavior becomes locally linear and therefore solvable.
depths.deep: In higher dimensions the derivative is a linear map (the Jacobian), not a number, and differentiability means the map approximates f with error o(‖h‖). The chain rule is then just composition of linear maps. Smoothness is a ladder: differentiable ⊂ continuously differentiable ⊂ analytic, and the inclusions are strict.

atoms.note: Differentiable implies continuous, but not the reverse — |x| is continuous at 0 yet has no derivative there.
atoms.art_prompt: a curve with a tangent line touching it at one point, and an inset showing the curve and line nearly coinciding when zoomed

quiz.prompt: State the derivative as a limit, and say what geometric object it computes.
quiz.answer: f'(a) = lim_{h→0} [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h; it is the slope of the tangent line, the instantaneous rate of change at a.

quiz.prompt: Use the limit definition to show the derivative of f(x) = x^2 is 2x.
quiz.answer: [ (x+h)^2 − x^2 ]/h = (2xh + h^2)/h = 2x + h, and as h→0 this tends to 2x.

atoms.title: The integral and the Fundamental Theorem
atoms.summary: The integral accumulates a function over an interval as a limit of sums; the Fundamental Theorem makes integration and differentiation inverse operations.

depths.eli5: Slice the area under a curve into thin rectangles, add them up, and let the slices get infinitely thin. The Fundamental Theorem says undoing a derivative gives you that area for free.
depths.core: The Riemann integral is the common limit of upper and lower rectangle sums as the partition is refined. Its deep partner, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, has two faces: differentiating an accumulation function returns the integrand, and integrating a derivative returns the net change f(b) − f(a). This duality is what makes calculus a calculus — a system for trading hard sums for antiderivatives.
depths.deep: Riemann integration fails for badly discontinuous functions and for interchanging limits; the Lebesgue integral repairs this by partitioning the range instead of the domain, giving the convergence theorems analysis needs. Measure theory is the price and the payoff.

atoms.note: The 'dx' is not decoration — it records the variable of integration and carries units, and it is what changes under substitution.
atoms.art_prompt: the area under a curve filled with rectangles that grow thinner and more numerous toward a smooth fill

quiz.prompt: What two operations does the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus relate, and how?
quiz.answer: Differentiation and integration — it states they are inverse operations: d/dx of an accumulation of f returns f, and integrating f' over [a,b] returns f(b) − f(a).

quiz.prompt: Using the Fundamental Theorem, evaluate the integral of 2x from 0 to 3.
quiz.answer: An antiderivative of 2x is x^2, so the value is 3^2 − 0^2 = 9.

atoms.title: Vector spaces
atoms.equation: u+v\in V,\quad \alpha v\in V,\quad \alpha(u+v)=\alpha u+\alpha v
atoms.summary: A vector space is a set where you can add elements and scale them by numbers, obeying distributive and associative rules. It is the arena of all of linear algebra.

depths.eli5: A vector space is a set of arrows you can add tip-to-tail and stretch by any number, and everything still lands inside the set. Functions, polynomials, and physical forces all qualify.
depths.core: Built on an abelian group (vectors under addition) plus a compatible scalar multiplication over a field, the eight axioms guarantee a basis exists: a minimal set whose linear combinations reach every vector uniquely. Dimension — the basis size — is then a complete invariant, so every n-dimensional space over a field looks exactly like coordinate n-space.
depths.deep: The leap of abstraction is that 'vector' need not mean arrow: solutions of a linear ODE, the polynomials of degree ≤ n, and the continuous functions on an interval are all vector spaces, so linear-algebraic reasoning transfers wholesale. Infinite-dimensional spaces need topology (completeness, norms) to behave, which is where functional analysis begins.

atoms.note: Subspaces must contain the zero vector — a line not through the origin is not a subspace.
atoms.art_prompt: two arrows from a common origin combining tip-to-tail into a third, with faint scaled copies of each

quiz.prompt: What is a basis of a vector space, and what does its size define?
quiz.answer: A linearly independent set that spans the space — every vector is a unique linear combination of it; its size is the dimension, a complete invariant of the space.

quiz.prompt: Is the set of polynomials of degree exactly 2 a vector space under the usual operations?
quiz.answer: No — it is not closed under addition (x^2 + (−x^2 + x) = x has degree 1) and lacks the zero polynomial; degree ≤ 2 is required to form a vector space.

atoms.title: Linear maps and matrices
atoms.summary: A linear map preserves addition and scaling; once a basis is fixed it is encoded by a matrix, and composition of maps becomes matrix multiplication.

depths.eli5: A linear map is a transformation that keeps grid lines straight and evenly spaced and keeps the origin fixed. A matrix is just its instruction sheet, one column per basis vector.
depths.core: Linearity — T respects sums and scalar multiples — means T is completely determined by where it sends a basis. Stacking those images as columns gives the matrix, and the rule (AB)v = A(Bv) makes matrix multiplication the bookkeeping of composing maps. The rank–nullity theorem (dim domain = rank + nullity) ties what the map crushes to zero to what it can reach.
depths.deep: Choosing a different basis conjugates the matrix by a change-of-basis matrix, so a matrix is a coordinate shadow of a basis-free object. Invariants that survive conjugation — rank, trace, determinant, eigenvalues — are the map's true properties; everything else is an artifact of the chosen coordinates.

atoms.note: Matrix multiplication is non-commutative because composing transformations in a different order generally lands you somewhere else.
atoms.art_prompt: a unit grid being sheared into a parallelogram grid with the origin pinned and basis vectors highlighted

quiz.prompt: Why does fixing a basis let you represent any linear map as a matrix?
quiz.answer: Linearity means the map is determined by its action on the basis vectors; placing each basis vector's image as a column builds the matrix, and linearity reconstructs the map on all inputs.

quiz.prompt: State the rank–nullity theorem and say what it constrains.
quiz.answer: dim(domain) = rank(T) + nullity(T); the dimension of the image plus the dimension of the kernel equals the input dimension, so a map cannot both collapse a lot and reach a lot.

atoms.title: Inner product spaces
atoms.summary: An inner product adds geometry — length and angle — to a vector space, defining orthogonality and enabling projection and best approximation.

depths.eli5: An inner product is a way to multiply two vectors into a single number that tells you how much they point the same way. Zero means perpendicular; that one idea unlocks distance and angle.
depths.core: A symmetric, positive-definite, bilinear (or Hermitian) form ⟨·,·⟩ defines a norm ‖v‖ = √⟨v,v⟩ and an angle via cos θ = ⟨u,v⟩/(‖u‖‖v‖), the last well-defined because the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds it. Orthogonal bases make projection trivial: the closest point in a subspace is the sum of projections onto its orthonormal directions — the engine of least squares and Fourier analysis.
depths.deep: Completeness turns an inner product space into a Hilbert space, where every closed subspace has an orthogonal complement and projection always exists. This single guarantee underwrites quantum mechanics (states as unit vectors, observables as self-adjoint operators) and signal processing alike.

atoms.note: Cauchy–Schwarz is what makes 'angle' meaningful — without it cos θ could exceed 1.
atoms.art_prompt: two vectors with a marked angle between them and a dashed projection of one onto the other

quiz.prompt: What does an inner product add to a bare vector space, and what does ⟨u,v⟩ = 0 mean?
quiz.answer: It adds geometry — a notion of length (norm) and angle; ⟨u,v⟩ = 0 means the two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular).

quiz.prompt: State the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and explain why it guarantees a valid angle between two vectors.
quiz.answer: |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖‖v‖; dividing gives |cos θ| = |⟨u,v⟩|/(‖u‖‖v‖) ≤ 1, so the ratio is a legitimate cosine and θ is well-defined.

atoms.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
atoms.summary: An eigenvector is a direction a linear map only stretches, never rotates; its eigenvalue is the stretch factor. They expose the map's intrinsic axes.

depths.eli5: Some special directions don't get knocked off course by a transformation — they just get longer or shorter. Those directions are eigenvectors, and the scaling number is the eigenvalue.
depths.core: Solving Av = λv finds directions preserved up to scaling. The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI) = 0; the eigenvectors span the corresponding invariant lines. When enough independent eigenvectors exist, the map is diagonalizable: in their basis it is just multiplication by the eigenvalues, so high powers and exponentials of the matrix become trivial.
depths.deep: Eigenvalues are basis-independent, so they are genuine invariants of the operator, and they govern dynamics: stability of fixed points, growth modes of linear ODE/recurrence systems, and resonance frequencies all read off the spectrum. Defective matrices (too few eigenvectors) need Jordan form, the structural footnote to diagonalization.

atoms.note: Real matrices can have complex eigenvalues — those encode rotation, with the magnitude giving the scaling and the argument the angle.
atoms.art_prompt: a transformed grid with two highlighted directions that stay on their own lines, one stretched and one shrunk

quiz.prompt: What geometric property distinguishes an eigenvector of A, and how do you find the eigenvalues?
quiz.answer: An eigenvector's direction is preserved by A (only scaled, not rotated); eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0.

quiz.prompt: Find the eigenvalues of the 2×2 matrix [[2,0],[0,3]] and explain why they are obvious here.
quiz.answer: It is diagonal, so det(A − λI) = (2−λ)(3−λ) = 0 gives λ = 2 and λ = 3; the standard basis vectors are already eigenvectors, scaled by 2 and 3.

atoms.title: Taylor's theorem
atoms.summary: Taylor's theorem approximates a smooth function near a point by a polynomial built from its derivatives, with an explicit remainder bounding the error.

depths.eli5: If you know a function's value and all its rates of change at one point, you can predict it nearby by adding polynomial corrections — slope, then curvature, then finer wiggles.
depths.core: Matching derivatives up to order n at a gives the best degree-n polynomial fit; the remainder R_n (Lagrange form: f^{(n+1)}(ξ)/(n+1)! · (x−a)^{n+1}) makes the approximation an equality and bounds how fast it degrades away from a. This is why linearization (n=1) and quadratic models (n=2) are everywhere — they are truncated Taylor series with controlled error.
depths.deep: When the remainder vanishes as n→∞ on an interval, the function equals its Taylor series there and is called analytic. Not all smooth functions are analytic — e^{−1/x^2} has every derivative zero at 0 yet is nonzero nearby — which is why real analysis and complex analysis diverge so sharply.

atoms.note: A Taylor series can converge yet converge to the wrong function — convergence and equality are separate questions, settled by the remainder.
atoms.art_prompt: a curve overlaid with progressively higher-degree polynomial approximations hugging it over a widening interval

quiz.prompt: What information about f at a point does the degree-n Taylor polynomial use, and what does the remainder term provide?
quiz.answer: The values of f and its first n derivatives at a; the remainder R_n gives the exact error, bounding how far the polynomial drifts from f away from a.

quiz.prompt: Write the degree-2 Taylor polynomial of e^x about 0 and use it to estimate e^{0.1}.

atoms.title: Metric spaces
atoms.summary: A metric space abstracts 'distance', letting limits, continuity, and convergence be defined far beyond the real line. The triangle inequality is its load-bearing axiom.

depths.eli5: A metric is any honest notion of distance: never negative, symmetric, and where a detour is never shorter than going direct. Once you have distance, 'getting close' — and therefore limits — makes sense anywhere.
depths.core: Three axioms (non-negativity with identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and the triangle inequality) are enough to define open balls, convergence, and continuity. This lets the same analysis run on function spaces, sequence spaces, and graphs, not just the reals. Completeness — every Cauchy sequence converges — is the extra property that makes a metric space safe for fixed-point and existence arguments.
depths.deep: Open sets defined by the metric generalize further to topology, where 'nearness' survives even without a distance. Compactness (every open cover has a finite subcover) is the property that rescues the intuition 'closed and bounded' carries on the reals, underwriting maxima, uniform continuity, and convergence of subsequences.

atoms.note: Different metrics on the same set can give the same open sets (topology) — distance is more data than nearness.
atoms.art_prompt: three points with edges labeled by distances, the direct edge visibly no longer than the two-edge detour

quiz.prompt: State the triangle inequality and explain why it is the crucial metric axiom.
quiz.answer: d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y) + d(y,z): a direct distance never exceeds a detour. It is what makes open balls and limits behave consistently, enabling continuity and convergence arguments.

quiz.prompt: What additional property must a metric space have for the Banach fixed-point (contraction mapping) theorem to apply, and why?
quiz.answer: Completeness — every Cauchy sequence must converge — so the iterates of the contraction, which form a Cauchy sequence, are guaranteed to have a limit point inside the space.

atoms.title: The spectral theorem
atoms.summary: Every self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues — it is diagonal in the right coordinates. This is the backbone of quantum mechanics and PCA.

depths.eli5: If a transformation is its own mirror image (symmetric), then it has a set of perpendicular axes it simply stretches along, with honest real stretch factors. Pick those axes and it becomes the simplest possible map.
depths.core: For a self-adjoint operator (A = A* — symmetric for real matrices, Hermitian for complex) the spectral theorem guarantees real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, so A decomposes as a sum of real eigenvalues times orthogonal projections. Geometrically every such map is a pure rescaling along perpendicular directions: no shear, no rotation, no defect.
depths.deep: This is why observables in quantum mechanics are self-adjoint — their real eigenvalues are the measurable outcomes and their orthogonal eigenstates the distinguishable results. The same theorem powers principal component analysis (diagonalizing a covariance matrix) and the stability analysis of symmetric systems. The infinite-dimensional version, requiring a spectral measure, is a cornerstone of functional analysis.

atoms.note: Self-adjointness is essential: a general matrix may not be diagonalizable at all, and a normal-but-not-self-adjoint one diagonalizes only over the complex numbers.
atoms.art_prompt: a symmetric transformation shown as pure stretching along three mutually perpendicular highlighted axes, no twisting

quiz.prompt: What does the spectral theorem guarantee for a self-adjoint operator?
quiz.answer: Real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors — equivalently, the operator is diagonalizable by an orthogonal/unitary change of basis into a sum of real eigenvalues times orthogonal projections.

quiz.prompt: Why must the eigenvalues of a quantum-mechanical observable be real, in terms of this theorem?
quiz.answer: Observables are modeled as self-adjoint operators, and the spectral theorem forces self-adjoint operators to have real eigenvalues — which is required because those eigenvalues are the physically measurable outcomes.

atoms.title: The generalized Stokes' theorem
atoms.summary: The integral of a differential form over a boundary equals the integral of its derivative over the interior. One identity unifies the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's, Gauss's, and the classical Stokes' theorems.

depths.eli5: What happens on the edge of a region is the sum of what happens inside it. Adding up tiny circulations or flows everywhere inside leaves only the boundary contributions, because interior walls cancel in pairs.
depths.core: Written with differential forms, every integral theorem of vector calculus is one statement: integrating dω over a region Ω equals integrating ω over its boundary ∂Ω. Setting the dimension appropriately recovers the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (1D), Green's theorem (2D), the divergence theorem, and the curl form of Stokes' theorem — they were never separate results.
depths.deep: The engine is that the boundary operator ∂ and the exterior derivative d are adjoint, and that ∂∂ = 0 mirrors dd = 0. This duality between boundaries and derivatives is the seed of de Rham cohomology, where 'closed forms modulo exact forms' detects the holes in a space — turning calculus into a probe of global topology.

atoms.note: The recurring miracle is cancellation: shared interior boundaries are traversed twice with opposite orientation and vanish, leaving only the outer edge.
sources: MIT OCW 18.952 Theory of Differential Forms
atoms.art_prompt: a region tiled with small oriented loops whose shared interior edges cancel, leaving one bold loop around the outer boundary

quiz.prompt: In one sentence, what does the generalized Stokes' theorem equate?
quiz.answer: The integral of a differential form ω over the boundary ∂Ω equals the integral of its exterior derivative dω over the region Ω.

quiz.prompt: Which classical theorem does the generalized Stokes' theorem reduce to in one dimension, and how?
quiz.answer: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: with Ω = [a,b] the boundary ∂Ω is the two endpoints {a,b} (with signs), so ∫_Ω df = ∫_{∂Ω} f becomes f(b) − f(a) = ∫_a^b f'.

atoms.title: Propositional logic and proof
atoms.summary: Logic fixes the rules for combining true/false statements and what counts as a valid deduction; a proof is a finite chain of such deductions from accepted premises.

depths.eli5: Statements are either true or false, and logic is the grammar for chaining them: 'if this, then that.' A proof is just a careful, step-by-step argument where each step follows from the ones before by an allowed rule.
depths.core: Propositional logic combines statements with not, and, or, implies, and iff, and assigns each compound a truth value from its parts. An argument is valid when the conclusion is true in every case the premises are. Core moves include modus ponens (from P and P⇒Q infer Q) and the contrapositive (P⇒Q is equivalent to ¬Q⇒¬P), the engine behind proof by contradiction.
depths.deep: Validity (truth in all interpretations) and provability (derivable by the rules) are distinct notions; Gödel's completeness theorem says for first-order logic they coincide — every semantically valid sentence has a finite proof. This soundness-and-completeness match is exactly what makes formal reasoning trustworthy, and its failure to extend to truth-in-arithmetic is the seed of incompleteness.

atoms.note: P⇒Q is false only when P is true and Q is false; a false premise makes the implication vacuously true.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: a truth table for P implies Q beside an arrow chain of statements each justified by a named rule

quiz.prompt: State the contrapositive of P ⇒ Q and explain why it is logically equivalent.
quiz.answer: The contrapositive is ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. Both are false in exactly the same single case (P true, Q false), so they have identical truth tables and are equivalent.

quiz.prompt: An implication P ⇒ Q has a false premise P. Is the implication true or false, and what is this called?
quiz.answer: True — it is vacuously true. An implication is only false when the premise is true and the conclusion false, so a false premise can never falsify it.

atoms.title: Quantifiers and induction
atoms.summary: Quantifiers (for all, there exists) let statements range over infinite domains; induction proves a 'for all natural numbers' claim by a base case plus a step that passes truth up the ladder.

depths.eli5: 'For all' and 'there exists' let one sentence speak about infinitely many things. Induction is like dominoes: knock over the first, show each domino topples the next, and they all fall.
depths.core: Predicate logic adds ∀ (universal) and ∃ (existential) quantifiers over a domain; their order matters — ∀x∃y differs from ∃y∀x. Mathematical induction proves ∀n P(n) over the naturals: verify the base P(0), then prove the inductive step P(n)⇒P(n+1). Strong induction assumes all smaller cases at once, which is equivalent but often handier.
depths.deep: Induction is logically equivalent to the well-ordering principle (every nonempty set of naturals has a least element) and is in fact one of the Peano axioms, not a theorem derivable without it. It is the finite human's lever on the actual infinite: a two-line argument certifies infinitely many cases.

atoms.note: The inductive step proves an implication, not P(n) itself — you assume P(n) freely as a hypothesis and only must deliver P(n+1).
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: a row of dominoes, the first being pushed and a glowing rule arrow from each domino to the next

quiz.prompt: What are the two parts of a proof by mathematical induction?
quiz.answer: A base case establishing P at the starting value, and an inductive step proving P(n) ⇒ P(n+1) for all n; together they yield P(n) for all n.

quiz.prompt: Why does swapping the quantifier order in 'for all x there exists y with y > x' change the meaning?
quiz.answer: ∀x∃y (y>x) is true over the reals (pick y depending on x), but ∃y∀x (y>x) claims one fixed y beats every x, which is false — order decides whether y may depend on x.

atoms.title: Sets, relations, and cardinality
atoms.summary: Modern mathematics is built on sets governed by axioms; relations and equivalence classes organize them, and bijections compare their sizes even when infinite.

depths.eli5: Everything in math can be packaged as a set. To compare two collections' sizes, try to pair them up one-to-one; if you can, they are the same size — even when both are endless.
depths.core: The Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms (with choice, ZFC) specify which sets exist and how to build new ones, dodging paradoxes like Russell's. Relations (subsets of A×B) capture pairings; an equivalence relation partitions a set into disjoint classes. Cardinality compares sizes by bijection: two sets are equinumerous exactly when a bijection exists between them.
depths.deep: Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals cannot be listed by the naturals, so |ℝ| > |ℕ| — there is a strict hierarchy of infinities. The continuum hypothesis (no cardinality strictly between them) is independent of ZFC, proven undecidable by Gödel and Cohen: the axioms genuinely do not settle it.

atoms.note: A proper class (like 'the collection of all sets') is too big to be a set — that restriction is what defuses Russell's paradox.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: two infinite columns of dots joined by one-to-one pairing arrows, with a diagonal stripe escaping any attempted list

quiz.prompt: When do two sets have the same cardinality, and how does this work for infinite sets?
quiz.answer: When a bijection exists between them; this criterion works for infinite sets too — e.g., the naturals and even numbers are equinumerous despite one containing the other.

quiz.prompt: Sketch why Cantor's diagonal argument shows the reals are uncountable.
quiz.answer: Assume the reals in (0,1) are listed. Build a new number differing from the n-th listed number in its n-th decimal digit; it differs from every listed number, so it was missing — no list can be complete.

atoms.title: Number systems: ℕ to ℂ
atoms.summary: Each number system is built to solve equations the previous one cannot: subtraction births the integers, division the rationals, limits the reals, and square roots of negatives the complex numbers.

depths.eli5: Start with counting numbers. Want to subtract freely? Add negatives. Divide freely? Add fractions. Fill in every gap on the line? Add the irrationals. Take the square root of −1? Add i. Each layer fixes a missing operation.
depths.core: ℕ supports addition and multiplication; ℤ closes subtraction; ℚ closes division (a field). But ℚ has gaps — √2 is missing — so ℝ is its completion, adding all limits of Cauchy sequences and the least-upper-bound property. ℝ still cannot solve x²=−1, so ℂ adjoins i with i²=−1, after which every polynomial factors completely.
depths.deep: The reals are the unique complete ordered field; completeness (no gaps) is exactly what makes calculus work. The complex numbers trade order for algebraic closure — you cannot order ℂ compatibly with its arithmetic, but you gain that every degree-n polynomial has n roots, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

atoms.note: ℝ is uncountable while ℚ is countable, so 'almost every' real number is irrational — the rationals are a measure-zero dusting on the line.
atoms.art_prompt: nested rings labeled N, Z, Q, R, C, each ring adding a missing operation noted on its edge

quiz.prompt: What operation or property forces each extension: ℤ from ℕ, ℚ from ℤ, ℝ from ℚ, and ℂ from ℝ?
quiz.answer: ℤ closes subtraction (negatives), ℚ closes division (inverses), ℝ closes limits/fills gaps (completeness), and ℂ closes square roots of negatives (algebraic closure).

quiz.prompt: What does the reals possess that the rationals lack, and why does calculus need it?
quiz.answer: Completeness — the least-upper-bound property, so every bounded sequence has the limits it should. Without it, expected limits (and √2) would be 'missing,' and limits/derivatives could fail to exist.

atoms.title: Modular arithmetic
atoms.summary: Modular arithmetic works with remainders after division by a fixed modulus, turning the integers into finite cyclic systems where clock-like wraparound is the rule.

depths.eli5: On a 12-hour clock, 13 o'clock is just 1 o'clock — numbers wrap around after they hit the modulus. Modular arithmetic does all of addition and multiplication this way, keeping only remainders.
depths.core: Two integers are congruent mod n when they leave the same remainder; this is an equivalence relation, and the classes form the ring ℤ/nℤ. Addition and multiplication respect congruence, so you can reduce at any step. When n is prime, ℤ/nℤ is a field — every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse — which underlies Fermat's little theorem.
depths.deep: The Chinese remainder theorem decomposes ℤ/mnℤ into ℤ/mℤ × ℤ/nℤ for coprime m,n, parallelizing computation. These finite structures are the backbone of public-key cryptography: RSA's security rests on modular exponentiation being easy while its inverse (factoring) is hard.

atoms.note: Division is delicate mod n: you can divide by a only if a is coprime to n, which is why prime moduli are so convenient.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: a clock face with numbers wrapping past 12 back to 1, arithmetic arrows looping around the dial

quiz.prompt: What does a ≡ b (mod n) mean, and when does ℤ/nℤ form a field?
quiz.answer: It means n divides a − b (same remainder mod n); ℤ/nℤ is a field exactly when n is prime, so every nonzero residue has a multiplicative inverse.

quiz.prompt: Compute 7 × 8 mod 5.

atoms.title: Polynomials and roots
atoms.summary: A polynomial is a finite sum of scaled powers; its roots are where it vanishes, and each root corresponds to a linear factor, linking algebra to geometry.

depths.eli5: A polynomial is a smooth curve built from powers of x added together. Its roots are where the curve crosses zero, and each crossing means you can peel off a simple factor like (x − r).
depths.core: The factor theorem says r is a root of p exactly when (x − r) divides p, so a degree-n polynomial has at most n roots. Polynomial division and the remainder theorem (p(r) is the remainder on dividing by x − r) make root-finding and factoring systematic. Over a field, polynomials form a ring with unique factorization into irreducibles, mirroring the integers.
depths.deep: Whether all roots are expressible by radicals depends on the symmetry group of the roots — Galois theory shows the general quintic has no radical formula because its symmetry group is not solvable. The roots' existence is guaranteed only after passing to ℂ, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

atoms.note: Counting roots with multiplicity is what makes 'degree-n has n roots' exact — a double root counts twice.
atoms.art_prompt: a polynomial curve crossing the x-axis at several points, each crossing tagged with its linear factor

quiz.prompt: State the factor theorem and the bound it gives on the number of roots.
quiz.answer: r is a root of p exactly when (x − r) divides p; consequently a degree-n polynomial has at most n roots (exactly n over ℂ, counted with multiplicity).

quiz.prompt: Factor x² − 5x + 6 by finding its roots.
quiz.answer: Its roots are 2 and 3 (they sum to 5 and multiply to 6), so x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3).

atoms.title: Counting and combinatorics
atoms.summary: Combinatorics is the art of counting arrangements and selections without listing them, built from the multiplication principle, permutations, and combinations.

depths.eli5: How many ways can you arrange or pick things? Combinatorics gives shortcuts so you never have to write them all out. Order-matters gives permutations; order-doesn't-matter gives combinations.
depths.core: The multiplication principle counts independent choices by multiplying their options. Permutations P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)! count ordered selections; combinations C(n,k) count unordered ones, the binomial coefficients. The binomial theorem (a+b)ⁿ = Σ C(n,k) aᵏbⁿ⁻ᵏ ties these counts to algebra, and inclusion–exclusion corrects for overcounted overlaps.
depths.deep: Combinatorial identities often have two proofs: an algebraic one and a bijective one that exhibits a size-preserving correspondence, the latter being more illuminating. Generating functions package an entire counting sequence into one formal power series, turning recurrences into algebra — the gateway to analytic combinatorics.

atoms.note: C(n,k) = C(n,n−k): choosing what to include is the same as choosing what to leave out.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: Pascal's triangle with one row highlighted and a small set showing the k chosen elements it counts

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a permutation and a combination, and which formula gives each?
quiz.answer: Permutations count ordered selections, P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)!; combinations count unordered selections, C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!) — order matters for the first, not the second.

quiz.prompt: How many ways are there to choose a 3-person committee from 6 people?

atoms.title: Probability axioms
atoms.summary: Probability assigns numbers in [0,1] to events under three axioms; from them flow conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' rule for updating belief.

depths.eli5: Probability measures how likely things are, from 0 (never) to 1 (always). The rules are simple: something must happen, chances can't be negative, and the chance of one of several non-overlapping things is the sum of their chances.
depths.core: Kolmogorov's axioms — non-negativity, total mass 1, and countable additivity over disjoint events — make probability a measure on a sample space. Conditional probability P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) restricts the world to B; independence is P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Bayes' rule, P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B), inverts conditionals and is the formal law of updating beliefs from evidence.
depths.deep: Random variables push probability onto the real line; their expectation is a Lebesgue integral against the distribution, which is why measure theory is the rigorous home of probability. The law of large numbers and central limit theorem then explain why averages stabilize and why the Gaussian appears everywhere.

atoms.note: Independence and disjointness are opposite extremes — disjoint nonzero-probability events are maximally dependent (one occurring forbids the other).
atoms.art_prompt: a sample-space rectangle of area one with overlapping event blobs, a conditional view zooming into one blob

quiz.prompt: State Bayes' rule and say what it lets you do.
quiz.answer: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B); it inverts a conditional probability, letting you update the probability of a cause A given observed evidence B.

quiz.prompt: If P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, and A,B are independent, what is P(A∩B)?
quiz.answer: Independence gives P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)=0.5×0.4=0.2.

atoms.title: Random variables and expectation
atoms.summary: A random variable turns outcomes into numbers; expectation is its probability-weighted average, and variance measures its spread, with linearity of expectation as the workhorse.

depths.eli5: A random variable is a number whose value depends on chance, like a die roll. Its expectation is the long-run average you'd see, and the variance says how wildly it swings around that average.
depths.core: A random variable X maps outcomes to numbers, with a distribution (pmf for discrete, pdf for continuous). Expectation E[X] is the weighted average; it is linear — E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] regardless of dependence — which makes many hard counts easy. Variance Var(X)=E[(X−E[X])²]=E[X²]−E[X]² quantifies spread, and standard deviation restores the units.
depths.deep: The law of large numbers says sample averages converge to E[X], and the central limit theorem says their fluctuations, rescaled by √n, become Gaussian regardless of the original distribution — which is why the normal curve is universal. These two theorems are the bridge from individual randomness to predictable aggregate behavior.

atoms.note: Linearity of expectation needs no independence — that is exactly what makes it so powerful for combinatorial counting.
atoms.art_prompt: a distribution histogram with a marked mean line and shaded one-standard-deviation band around it

quiz.prompt: Why is linearity of expectation so useful, and what condition does it require?
quiz.answer: E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y] always holds, with no independence required, so you can split a complicated random quantity into simple pieces and add their averages.

quiz.prompt: A fair die is rolled. What is the expected value of the result?

atoms.title: Rings and fields
atoms.summary: A ring has two compatible operations — addition (a group) and multiplication (associative, distributing over addition); a field is a ring where every nonzero element is invertible.

depths.eli5: A ring is a number system where you can add, subtract, and multiply — like the integers. A field is a ring where you can also divide by anything nonzero — like the rationals or reals. The two operations must play nicely via distribution.
depths.core: A ring is an abelian group under addition plus an associative multiplication that distributes over addition. Commutative rings with a multiplicative identity (like ℤ and polynomial rings) are the setting for most arithmetic. A field strengthens this so multiplication is also a group on the nonzero elements — every nonzero element has an inverse — giving ℚ, ℝ, ℂ, and ℤ/pℤ.
depths.deep: Ideals are the ring-theoretic analog of normal subgroups; quotient rings R/I generalize modular arithmetic, and an ideal is maximal exactly when the quotient is a field. This machinery (ideals, quotients, homomorphisms) is the unified language behind number theory, algebraic geometry, and coding theory.

atoms.note: Every field is a ring, but ℤ is a ring that is not a field — it lacks inverses for everything except ±1.
atoms.art_prompt: two operation tables side by side, addition forming a full group and multiplication a group only after removing zero

quiz.prompt: What single property separates a field from a general commutative ring with identity?
quiz.answer: In a field every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse (you can divide); a general ring need not have this — e.g., ℤ.

quiz.prompt: Is ℤ/6ℤ a field? Why or why not?
quiz.answer: No — 6 is not prime, so 2 and 3 are nonzero yet 2×3 ≡ 0; zero divisors exist and 2 has no inverse, so it fails to be a field.

atoms.title: Homomorphisms and quotients
atoms.summary: A homomorphism is a structure-preserving map between algebraic objects; its kernel measures what it collapses, and the isomorphism theorem says the quotient by the kernel is a faithful copy of the image.

depths.eli5: A homomorphism is a translation between two systems that keeps the arithmetic intact: multiply then translate, or translate then multiply, and you land in the same place. What it crushes to the identity is its 'kernel,' and that crushing is exactly how much information it loses.
depths.core: A homomorphism φ respects the operation: φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b). Its kernel (elements sent to the identity) is a normal subgroup (or ideal); its image is a substructure. The first isomorphism theorem, G/ker φ ≅ im φ, says quotienting out exactly what the map forgets recovers a perfect copy of what it sees — collapsing and embedding are two views of one map.
depths.deep: This is the organizing principle of algebra: classify objects up to isomorphism, and understand every map as an embedding composed with a quotient. Functorially, taking kernels and cokernels and asking when sequences are exact generalizes into homological algebra, which exports the same bookkeeping to topology and geometry.

atoms.note: Normality of the kernel is not optional — it is precisely the condition that makes the quotient G/ker φ a group at all.
atoms.art_prompt: a map folding a large group onto a smaller one, all elements of one fiber collapsing to a single image point

quiz.prompt: What does the first isomorphism theorem state?
quiz.answer: For a homomorphism φ: G→H, the quotient G/ker φ is isomorphic to the image im φ — quotienting by what the map collapses gives a faithful copy of what it produces.

quiz.prompt: What does it mean if a homomorphism's kernel is trivial (just the identity)?
quiz.answer: The map is injective: distinct elements stay distinct, since only the identity maps to the identity, so G embeds as a copy inside the target.

atoms.title: Complex numbers and Euler's formula
atoms.summary: Complex numbers extend the reals with i (√−1); Euler's formula fuses the exponential with trigonometry, revealing rotation and oscillation as one phenomenon.

depths.eli5: Add a new number i whose square is −1, and suddenly every equation has solutions. Plotting these numbers on a plane, multiplying by i is a quarter turn — so complex multiplication is rotation, and that's why waves and circles speak its language.
depths.core: A complex number a+bi lives in the plane, with modulus |z| (length) and argument arg z (angle). Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments, making rotation algebraic. Euler's formula e^{iθ}=cos θ + i sin θ — provable by matching Taylor series — packages all of trigonometry into the exponential, and the special case e^{iπ}+1=0 links five fundamental constants.
depths.deep: Functions of a complex variable that are differentiable (holomorphic) are automatically infinitely differentiable and equal to their power series — rigidity with no real-variable analog. This is why complex analysis yields the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, contour-integral evaluations of real integrals, and the analytic continuation that defines the Riemann zeta function.

atoms.note: Raising to powers and extracting roots become trivial in polar form via de Moivre's theorem — the n-th roots of unity are equally spaced points on the unit circle.
atoms.art_prompt: the complex plane with a unit vector at angle theta, its cos and sin components dropped to the axes

quiz.prompt: State Euler's formula and explain geometrically what multiplying by e^{iθ} does.
quiz.answer: e^{iθ}=cos θ + i sin θ; multiplying by it rotates a complex number counterclockwise by angle θ about the origin without changing its length.

quiz.prompt: Use Euler's formula to evaluate e^{iπ}.
quiz.answer: e^{iπ} = cos π + i sin π = −1 + 0 = −1, giving the identity e^{iπ} + 1 = 0.

atoms.title: Sequences and series
atoms.summary: A series is the limit of partial sums of a sequence; convergence tests decide when infinitely many terms add to a finite total, with absolute convergence being the well-behaved case.

depths.eli5: Add up infinitely many shrinking numbers — sometimes the total settles on a finite value, sometimes it blows up. There are tests to tell which, and the geometric series (each term a fixed fraction of the last) is the model example.
depths.core: A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums approach a limit. The geometric series sums to 1/(1−r) for |r|<1; the ratio and root tests compare growth to a geometric benchmark; comparison and integral tests pin down others. Absolute convergence (Σ|aₙ| converges) guarantees the sum is unchanged by reordering — conditional convergence does not.
depths.deep: Riemann's rearrangement theorem shows a conditionally convergent series (like the alternating harmonic series) can be reordered to sum to any real number, or to diverge — proving that infinite addition is not blindly commutative. Power series, convergent on a disk, are the bridge to Taylor expansions and complex analysis.

atoms.note: The harmonic series Σ1/n diverges even though its terms go to zero — terms vanishing is necessary but never sufficient for convergence.
atoms.art_prompt: a bar chart of shrinking terms stacking up to a horizontal asymptote line marking the finite sum

quiz.prompt: What is the sum of the geometric series 1 + r + r² + ... for |r| < 1, and what happens if |r| ≥ 1?
quiz.answer: It sums to 1/(1−r) when |r|<1; for |r|≥1 the terms don't shrink to zero, so the series diverges.

quiz.prompt: Does Σ 1/n² converge, and what test settles it most cleanly?
quiz.answer: Yes — the integral test compares it to ∫1/x² dx, which is finite, so the series converges (in fact to π²/6).

atoms.title: Gradient, divergence, and curl
atoms.equation: \nabla f=\Big(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial x},\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial y},\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}\Big)
atoms.summary: Multivariable calculus extends differentiation to fields: the gradient points uphill steepest, divergence measures outflow, and curl measures rotation.

depths.eli5: On a hilly landscape, the gradient is the arrow pointing straight uphill, as steep as possible. For a flowing fluid, divergence tells you where it's spreading out and curl tells you where it's swirling.
depths.core: Partial derivatives measure change in one direction; the gradient ∇f assembles them into the vector of steepest ascent, perpendicular to level sets. For a vector field, divergence ∇·F is the net rate of outflow per volume (sources and sinks) and curl ∇×F is the local rotation. These three operators built from ∇ organize all of vector calculus.
depths.deep: Identities like curl(grad f)=0 and div(curl F)=0 are not coincidences — they are the statement d²=0 for differential forms, and they encode that conservative fields have potentials and that what circulates has no net source. This is the local face of the generalized Stokes' theorem.

atoms.note: The gradient is always perpendicular to the level set through a point — which is why it gives the direction of fastest increase.
atoms.art_prompt: a contour map with gradient arrows crossing contours perpendicularly toward higher ground, plus a small swirl marked as curl

quiz.prompt: What does the gradient of a scalar field point toward, and how does it relate to level sets?
quiz.answer: It points in the direction of steepest increase of the function, and it is always perpendicular to the level sets (contours) of that function.

quiz.prompt: Compute the gradient of f(x,y) = x²y at the point (1,2).

atoms.title: Ordinary differential equations
atoms.summary: An ODE relates a function to its derivatives; solving one finds the function whose rate of change obeys a given law, with existence and uniqueness guaranteed under mild conditions.

depths.eli5: An ODE says how fast something changes in terms of where it currently is. Solving it reconstructs the whole history from that rule — like predicting a population's growth from its growth rate.
depths.core: A first-order ODE y'=f(t,y) prescribes the slope at every point; the solution is a curve threading that slope field. Linear ODEs with constant coefficients solve via exponentials e^{λt} whose exponents are roots of the characteristic polynomial. The Picard–Lindelöf theorem guarantees a unique solution through each initial point when f is Lipschitz in y.
depths.deep: Systems of ODEs y'=Ay solve by diagonalizing A — eigenvalues set growth/decay rates and oscillation frequencies, tying dynamics directly to the spectrum. Nonlinear ODEs rarely solve in closed form, so the qualitative theory (fixed points, stability, phase portraits) and numerical integration take over; sensitive dependence here is the doorway to chaos.

atoms.note: The exponential function is the eigenfunction of differentiation (d/dt of e^{λt} is λe^{λt}), which is why linear ODEs are solved by exponentials.
atoms.art_prompt: a slope field of short tilted segments with one solution curve flowing tangent to them from an initial dot

quiz.prompt: Solve y' = ky and state the role of the initial condition.
quiz.answer: y = y₀e^{kt}; the initial value y₀ = y(0) fixes the single constant of integration, selecting one curve from the family of solutions.

quiz.prompt: What does the Picard–Lindelöf theorem guarantee, and what condition does it need?
quiz.answer: A unique solution through each initial point, provided f(t,y) is continuous and Lipschitz continuous in y near that point.

atoms.title: Fourier series and transform
atoms.summary: Fourier analysis decomposes a function into pure frequencies; periodic signals become discrete series and general ones become a continuous spectrum, with the basis being orthogonal exponentials.

depths.eli5: Any signal — a sound, a wave, an image — can be broken into pure tones of different frequencies, like splitting white light into a rainbow. The Fourier transform is the prism that tells you how much of each frequency is present.
depths.core: On an interval, the complex exponentials e^{2πinx} form an orthonormal basis, so a periodic function is a sum of them — its Fourier series — with coefficients given by inner products. For non-periodic functions the sum becomes the Fourier transform integral, mapping a function to its frequency content. Differentiation becomes multiplication by frequency, turning differential equations into algebra.
depths.deep: Fourier analysis is the spectral theorem for the differentiation operator: the exponentials are its eigenfunctions. Plancherel's theorem says the transform preserves energy (the L² norm), making it a unitary map. The uncertainty principle — a function and its transform cannot both be sharply localized — is a theorem here, not just physics.

atoms.note: Convolution in one domain is plain multiplication in the other — the property that makes the transform the backbone of signal processing and PDE solving.
atoms.art_prompt: a complicated waveform splitting via a prism into a stack of pure sine waves of increasing frequency

quiz.prompt: What basis does a Fourier series expand a periodic function in, and why is orthogonality essential?
quiz.answer: The complex exponentials (equivalently sines and cosines); orthogonality lets each coefficient be extracted independently via an inner product, with no cross-contamination between frequencies.

quiz.prompt: Why does the Fourier transform simplify solving linear differential equations?
quiz.answer: It converts differentiation into multiplication by frequency (×2πiξ), turning a differential equation into an algebraic one in the frequency domain that you solve and transform back.

atoms.title: Topological spaces
atoms.summary: Topology axiomatizes 'nearness' through open sets alone, abstracting away distance; it captures the properties of shape that survive continuous deformation, like connectedness and compactness.

depths.eli5: Topology is geometry without rulers — it only cares which points are 'near' which, not how far. A coffee mug and a donut are the same to a topologist because one can be reshaped into the other without tearing.
depths.core: A topology is a collection of 'open' subsets closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections, with the whole space and empty set included. Continuity is defined purely by open sets (preimages of opens are open), needing no metric. The key invariants — connectedness (no splitting into two opens), compactness (every open cover has a finite subcover), and the Hausdorff separation property — classify spaces up to homeomorphism.
depths.deep: Compactness is the topological essence of 'closed and bounded' and is what makes continuous functions on a space attain maxima and behave; the Heine–Borel theorem says it coincides with closed-and-bounded only in finite-dimensional spaces. Algebraic invariants like the fundamental group and homology turn these qualitative shape questions into computable algebra.

atoms.note: Every metric space is a topological space (the metric defines the opens), but not every topology comes from a metric — topology is strictly more general.
atoms.art_prompt: a coffee mug morphing continuously into a donut, with open-set blobs covering the surface as it deforms

quiz.prompt: How is continuity defined in topology without reference to distance?
quiz.answer: A map is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open; this recovers the metric notion of continuity using only the open-set structure.

quiz.prompt: What does compactness guarantee for a continuous real-valued function on a compact space?
quiz.answer: The function attains a maximum and minimum value (the extreme value theorem); its image is also compact, hence closed and bounded.

atoms.title: Determinants
atoms.summary: The determinant is the signed volume-scaling factor of a linear map; it is zero exactly when the map collapses dimension, signaling non-invertibility.

depths.eli5: Feed a unit box through a transformation and see what volume comes out; the determinant is that volume (with a sign for flips). If it's zero, the box got squashed flat and the transformation can't be undone.
depths.core: The determinant is the unique function on square matrices that is linear in each column, alternating (swapping columns negates it), and equals 1 on the identity. Geometrically it is the factor by which the map scales oriented volume. Multiplicativity det(AB)=det A·det B mirrors composition, and det A = 0 exactly characterizes singular (non-invertible) maps with nontrivial kernel.
depths.deep: Determinants drive the characteristic polynomial det(A−λI) and hence eigenvalues, the Jacobian's role in the multivariable change-of-variables formula, and Cramer's rule. The sign tracks orientation, distinguishing rotations from reflections — the algebraic seed of orientation in geometry and topology.

atoms.note: det A = 0 means columns are linearly dependent — the map flattens space, so volume vanishes and inversion is impossible.
atoms.art_prompt: a unit square transformed into a parallelogram with its area labeled as the determinant, and a degenerate flat case at det zero

quiz.prompt: What does the determinant tell you geometrically, and what does det A = 0 imply?
quiz.answer: It is the signed factor by which the map scales volume; det A = 0 means the map collapses dimension, the columns are dependent, and A is not invertible.

quiz.prompt: Compute the determinant of [[1,2],[3,4]] and say whether the matrix is invertible.
quiz.answer: det = 1·4 − 2·3 = 4 − 6 = −2 ≠ 0, so the matrix is invertible.

atoms.title: Completeness and uniform convergence
atoms.summary: Real analysis rigorizes calculus: completeness of ℝ makes limits exist, and uniform convergence is the condition that lets you swap limits with integrals and derivatives.

depths.eli5: Calculus works because the real line has no holes — every sequence that 'should' converge actually does. And when a family of functions settles to a limit evenly everywhere at once, you can safely integrate or differentiate the limit.
depths.core: Completeness (every Cauchy sequence converges) is the axiom distinguishing ℝ from ℚ and underwrites the existence of suprema, limits, and integrals. Pointwise convergence is too weak — limit and integral can disagree — but uniform convergence (one rate of approach for all points) lets you interchange the limit with integration and, with care, differentiation. This control is what separates rigorous analysis from formal manipulation.
depths.deep: The pathologies that motivated analysis — functions continuous nowhere differentiable (Weierstrass), series whose term-by-term derivative diverges — show that intuition fails without uniform control. The Arzelà–Ascoli and dominated convergence theorems are the heavier tools that grant limit interchange under weaker hypotheses, leading into measure theory.

atoms.note: Pointwise limits of continuous functions can be discontinuous; uniform limits cannot — uniformity preserves continuity.
atoms.art_prompt: a sequence of curves nested inside a shrinking tube around their limit, contrasted with curves that converge only at scattered points

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between pointwise and uniform convergence, and why does it matter?
quiz.answer: Pointwise: each point converges at its own rate. Uniform: a single rate works for all points at once. Uniformity is what lets you interchange the limit with integrals/derivatives and preserves continuity.

quiz.prompt: Why does completeness of ℝ, but not ℚ, make it suitable for calculus?
quiz.answer: In ℝ every Cauchy sequence converges (no gaps), so limits, suprema, and integrals always exist; in ℚ a Cauchy sequence can approach √2, which is missing, so expected limits fail to exist.

atoms.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
atoms.summary: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root; equivalently ℂ is algebraically closed, so every degree-n polynomial factors into n linear pieces.

depths.eli5: Once you allow complex numbers, every polynomial equation can be solved — there are no more 'unsolvable' ones. A degree-n polynomial always splits completely into n simple factors.
depths.core: The theorem states ℂ is algebraically closed: any polynomial of degree ≥ 1 with complex coefficients has at least one root in ℂ, and by induction factors completely into linear terms (with multiplicity, exactly n roots). This is why ℂ, not ℝ, is the natural home of algebra — the search for roots that began at √−1 terminates here.
depths.deep: Strikingly, every proof needs analysis or topology — purely algebraic methods cannot reach it, because the result is about ℂ's topological completeness. Liouville's theorem (a bounded entire function is constant) gives the slickest proof: if p had no root, 1/p would be bounded and entire, hence constant, contradicting deg p ≥ 1. The result is the keystone joining algebra, analysis, and topology.

atoms.note: It guarantees existence, not a formula — Galois theory shows degree-5+ polynomials generally have no solution by radicals even though the roots provably exist.
atoms.art_prompt: a degree-five complex polynomial's five roots marked in the complex plane with linear factors peeling off one by one

quiz.prompt: State the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra in terms of algebraic closure.
quiz.answer: ℂ is algebraically closed: every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root, hence factors into exactly deg p linear factors counted with multiplicity.

quiz.prompt: Sketch the Liouville-theorem proof that a non-constant complex polynomial must have a root.
quiz.answer: If p had no root, 1/p would be entire and bounded (it decays at infinity), so by Liouville it is constant, forcing p constant — contradicting deg p ≥ 1. Hence p has a root.

atoms.title: The Central Limit Theorem
atoms.summary: The normalized sum of many independent, finite-variance random variables converges to a Gaussian, regardless of their individual distributions — explaining why the bell curve is everywhere.

depths.eli5: Add up lots of independent random nudges and the total, once you center and rescale it, always looks like the same bell-shaped curve — no matter what the individual nudges looked like. That universality is why the bell curve shows up across nature.
depths.core: For independent, identically distributed variables with mean μ and finite variance σ², the standardized sum (Sₙ − nμ)/(σ√n) converges in distribution to the standard normal as n→∞. The original distribution's shape is washed out; only its mean and variance survive. This is the deep reason measurement errors, and many aggregates, are approximately Gaussian.
depths.deep: The cleanest proof uses characteristic functions: the Fourier transform of the rescaled sum converges pointwise to e^{−t²/2}, the Gaussian's transform, and Lévy's continuity theorem converts that into convergence in distribution. The Gaussian is a fixed point of this averaging-and-rescaling flow — it is the attractor, which generalizes to stable laws when variance is infinite.

atoms.note: Finite variance is essential — heavy-tailed distributions (like Cauchy) violate the hypothesis and converge to non-Gaussian stable laws instead.
atoms.art_prompt: histograms of sums of more and more dice rolls, each smoother, converging to an overlaid bell curve

quiz.prompt: What does the Central Limit Theorem say about sums of independent random variables, and what hypothesis is essential?
quiz.answer: Their standardized sum converges to a standard normal distribution regardless of the underlying distribution; the key hypothesis is finite (nonzero) variance.

quiz.prompt: Why is the average of many independent measurement errors approximately Gaussian?
quiz.answer: Each error is an independent random variable with finite variance; by the CLT their normalized sum (hence their average) converges to a Gaussian, washing out the individual error shapes.

atoms.title: Computability and the halting problem
atoms.summary: A Turing machine formalizes 'effective computation'; the halting problem proves some well-posed questions are undecidable — no algorithm can decide them all.

depths.eli5: A computer is, in essence, a simple rule-following machine. Some questions — like 'will this program eventually stop?' — sound answerable, but no program can answer them for all programs. There's a hard wall on what computation can ever do.
depths.core: The Turing machine (equivalently the lambda calculus, by the Church–Turing thesis) defines what 'computable' means. The halting problem asks for an algorithm H deciding whether an arbitrary program P halts on input x. A diagonal argument shows no such H exists: assuming one, build a program that halts exactly when H says it loops, a contradiction. Undecidability is thus a mathematical fact, not an engineering limit.
depths.deep: Undecidability spreads by reduction: any problem to which halting reduces is also undecidable, sweeping in program equivalence, Hilbert's tenth problem (integer solutions to polynomials), and more. Computability sits beneath complexity theory (P vs NP asks how hard the decidable problems are) and is the constructive twin of Gödel incompleteness — both are diagonal arguments about self-reference.

atoms.note: The same diagonal trick — feeding a machine its own description — drives Cantor's uncountability, Gödel's theorems, and Russell's paradox.
sources: MIT OCW 6.045 Automata, Computability, and Complexity
atoms.art_prompt: a program reading its own source code as input, a decision box trying to predict its halting and contradicting itself

quiz.prompt: What does the halting problem assert is impossible?
quiz.answer: No single algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether that program eventually halts; the halting problem is undecidable.

quiz.prompt: Sketch the diagonal contradiction behind the halting problem's undecidability.
quiz.answer: Assume a decider H exists. Build D that, on input P, halts if H says P(P) loops and loops if H says P(P) halts. Running D(D) makes D halt iff it loops — a contradiction, so H cannot exist.

atoms.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
atoms.summary: Any consistent, effectively axiomatized theory rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency — a permanent limit on formal systems.

depths.eli5: Pick any consistent set of math rules powerful enough to do ordinary arithmetic. Gödel showed there will always be true statements those rules can never prove — and the system can never certify its own freedom from contradiction. You can't axiomatize all of truth.
depths.core: The first theorem: any consistent, recursively axiomatized theory T that can express basic arithmetic is incomplete — there is a sentence G, neither provable nor refutable in T, that is nonetheless true (it encodes 'I am not provable in T'). The second theorem: such a T cannot prove its own consistency. Together they end Hilbert's dream of a complete, self-certifying formal foundation for mathematics.
depths.deep: The mechanism is arithmetization: Gödel numbered formulas and proofs so that 'provable' became an arithmetic predicate, then built a self-referential sentence by diagonalization — the same self-reference behind the halting problem. Incompleteness is not a defect to be patched; adding G as an axiom yields a new theory with its own unprovable truths. The limit is structural and permanent for any sufficiently expressive, mechanically checkable system.

atoms.note: Incompleteness needs the theory to be both consistent and effectively axiomatized (machine-checkable proofs) and to encode arithmetic — drop any one and the conclusion can fail.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
atoms.art_prompt: a formal proof system depicted as a sealed machine with one true statement floating outside its reach, labeled unprovable

quiz.prompt: What do Gödel's two incompleteness theorems say, and what kind of theory do they apply to?
quiz.answer: First: any consistent, effectively axiomatized theory that can express arithmetic has true but unprovable statements. Second: such a theory cannot prove its own consistency. They apply to recursively axiomatizable, consistent theories rich enough for arithmetic.

quiz.prompt: Explain to a student why adding the unprovable Gödel sentence as a new axiom does not 'fix' incompleteness.
quiz.answer: The enlarged theory is still consistent, effectively axiomatized, and expresses arithmetic, so the theorem applies again: it has its own new Gödel sentence. Incompleteness recurs at every stage — it is structural, not a single missing axiom.

atoms.title: Categories, functors, and universal properties
atoms.summary: Category theory studies mathematical structures through their structure-preserving maps rather than their internals; functors translate between categories and universal properties define objects by their relationships.

depths.eli5: Instead of looking inside mathematical objects, category theory watches how they map to one another — the arrows between them. From the pattern of arrows alone you can pin down what an object is, like identifying a person purely by their relationships.
depths.core: A category is objects plus composable arrows (morphisms) with identities and associative composition — sets-and-functions, groups-and-homomorphisms, and spaces-and-continuous-maps are all examples. A functor maps one category to another, preserving composition and identities. Universal properties (products, limits, free objects) characterize a construction uniquely by a mapping-out or mapping-in condition, so the same definition recurs across all of mathematics.
depths.deep: Natural transformations are maps between functors, and the Yoneda lemma — an object is fully determined by the maps into it — formalizes 'you are who you relate to.' Adjunctions capture optimal one-sided inverses (free/forgetful pairs) and unify constructions from logic to topology. Category theory is the language in which analogies between fields become theorems, the connective tissue of modern foundations.

atoms.note: The slogan 'it's all about the arrows' is literal — categorical definitions never inspect the elements of an object, only its morphisms.
sources: MIT OCW 18.S996 Category Theory for Scientists
atoms.art_prompt: two dotted regions (categories) of nodes-and-arrows with a functor mapping nodes and arrows from one onto the other, structure preserved

quiz.prompt: What are the two ingredients of a category, and what must a functor preserve?
quiz.answer: Objects and morphisms (arrows) with associative composition and identities; a functor preserves composition and identity arrows when mapping one category to another.

quiz.prompt: Explain what it means to define an object by a universal property, using the example of a product.
quiz.answer: A product of A and B is defined not by its internal elements but by a mapping property: any object with maps to A and B factors uniquely through it. This characterizes the product up to unique isomorphism by relationships alone, so the same definition works in any category.

atoms.title: Trigonometry and the unit circle
atoms.summary: Trigonometric functions encode the coordinates of a point moving around the unit circle, turning angles into ratios and making periodic phenomena measurable.

depths.eli5: Walk around a circle of radius one and track your shadow on each axis: that's cosine (horizontal) and sine (vertical). Because you keep looping the circle, these functions repeat forever, which is how we describe anything that cycles.
depths.core: On the unit circle, cos θ and sin θ are the x and y coordinates at angle θ, so the Pythagorean identity sin²θ+cos²θ=1 is just the circle's equation. The functions are periodic with period 2π, and the angle-addition formulas express cos(α+β) and sin(α+β) in terms of the parts — the algebraic backbone of rotation and wave superposition.
depths.deep: Trigonometry is complex exponentials in disguise: cos θ and sin θ are the real and imaginary parts of e^{iθ}, so every trig identity is an exponential identity, and angle-addition is just e^{i(α+β)}=e^{iα}e^{iβ}. Radian measure is the natural choice because it makes d/dθ sin θ = cos θ exactly, with no stray constant.

atoms.note: Radians, not degrees, are mandatory in calculus — they are what make the derivative of sine equal cosine without a conversion factor.
atoms.art_prompt: a unit circle with a radius at angle theta, its horizontal and vertical projections labeled cosine and sine

quiz.prompt: Why is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, geometrically?
quiz.answer: cos θ and sin θ are the x and y coordinates of a point on the unit circle, so the identity is just the circle's equation x² + y² = 1.

quiz.prompt: What are cos(π/2) and sin(π/2), and where is that point on the unit circle?
quiz.answer: cos(π/2) = 0 and sin(π/2) = 1; the point is at the top of the circle, (0, 1).

atoms.title: Exponentials and logarithms
atoms.summary: The exponential turns addition into multiplication and is its own derivative; the logarithm inverts it, turning multiplication back into addition and taming growth across scales.

depths.eli5: Exponential growth means multiplying by the same factor over and over — it explodes fast. The logarithm is the undo button: it answers 'how many times did I multiply?' and compresses huge ranges into manageable numbers.
depths.core: The exponential function e^x is the unique function equal to its own derivative with value 1 at 0, so it solves y'=y; it converts sums to products (e^{a+b}=e^a e^b). Its inverse, the natural logarithm, converts products to sums (ln(ab)=ln a+ln b) and has derivative 1/x. Any exponential growth or decay process — compound interest, radioactive decay, population — is governed by these.
depths.deep: The number e arises as the limit (1+1/n)ⁿ and as the base making the growth rate equal the amount. Logarithms underlie information theory (bits are log₂ counts), entropy, and the slide-rule-era reduction of multiplication to addition; extending the exponential to complex arguments via Euler's formula unifies growth with oscillation.

atoms.note: Different bases differ only by a constant factor (logₐ x = ln x / ln a), so 'the' logarithm is the natural one up to scaling.
atoms.art_prompt: an exponential curve rising steeply beside its mirror-image logarithm curve, reflected across the line y equals x

quiz.prompt: What property makes e^x special among exponential functions, and what does the logarithm do to products?
quiz.answer: e^x is its own derivative (and equals 1 at 0), so it solves y'=y; the logarithm turns products into sums, ln(ab)=ln a + ln b.

quiz.prompt: Solve 2^x = 8 using logarithms.
quiz.answer: Take log base 2: x = log₂ 8 = 3, since 2³ = 8.

atoms.title: Intermediate, extreme, and mean value theorems
atoms.summary: These existence theorems guarantee that continuous and differentiable functions hit intermediate values, attain extremes on closed intervals, and somewhere match their average rate of change.

depths.eli5: If you start below a line and end above it, somewhere you crossed it (intermediate value). On a closed stretch a continuous trip has a highest and lowest point (extreme value). And over any trip your speedometer must read the average speed at least once (mean value).
depths.core: The intermediate value theorem says a continuous function on [a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b) — the basis of root-finding. The extreme value theorem says a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains a max and min. The mean value theorem says a differentiable function has a point where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a), the engine linking derivatives to global behavior.
depths.deep: These are not computational tricks but consequences of completeness and compactness: IVT relies on connectedness of the interval, EVT on its compactness, and MVT on Rolle's theorem plus differentiability. The MVT is what proves that zero derivative implies constant, that the sign of f' controls monotonicity, and ultimately underwrites the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

atoms.note: Drop continuity or closed-and-bounded and these fail — 1/x on (0,1] attains no maximum, showing why the hypotheses are load-bearing.
atoms.art_prompt: a curve crossing a horizontal target level, touching its highest point, and a tangent line drawn parallel to the secant from a to b

quiz.prompt: State the mean value theorem and one consequence of it.
quiz.answer: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some c in (a,b) has f'(c) = (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a). A consequence: if f'=0 everywhere, f is constant.

quiz.prompt: Use the intermediate value theorem to argue x³ + x − 1 = 0 has a real root in (0,1).
quiz.answer: At x=0 the value is −1 (negative) and at x=1 it is 1 (positive); the function is continuous, so by the IVT it must equal 0 somewhere in (0,1).

atoms.title: Optimization and convexity
atoms.summary: Optimization finds extrema by setting the derivative to zero; convexity is the structural condition guaranteeing such critical points are global minima and that descent methods converge.

depths.eli5: To find the lowest point of a valley, look where the ground is flat — that's where the slope is zero. If the valley is bowl-shaped (convex), the one flat spot is guaranteed to be the true bottom, and rolling downhill always finds it.
depths.core: At an interior extremum the gradient vanishes (∇f=0); the second-derivative (Hessian) test classifies the critical point.
