Convex functions — those lying below their chords, with positive-semidefinite Hessian — have no spurious local minima: every stationary point is a global minimum. Constrained problems use Lagrange multipliers, equating the objective's gradient to a combination of constraint gradients.
depths.deep: Convexity is what makes large-scale optimization tractable: gradient descent and its variants provably converge for convex objectives, and duality turns a hard constrained problem into a paired one with the same optimum. Modern machine learning lives in the non-convex regime, where these guarantees weaken and the geometry of saddle points and overparameterization takes over.

atoms.note: A zero gradient marks a critical point, not necessarily a minimum — it could be a maximum or a saddle; convexity is what removes that ambiguity.
atoms.art_prompt: a convex bowl surface with a ball at the single flat bottom, beside a wavy non-convex surface trapping a ball in a false dip

quiz.prompt: What condition holds at an interior extremum, and what does convexity add?
quiz.answer: The gradient (or derivative) is zero there; convexity guarantees that any such stationary point is a global minimum, with no other local minima to get stuck in.

quiz.prompt: Find and classify the critical point of f(x) = x² − 4x + 7.
quiz.answer: f'(x)=2x−4=0 gives x=2; f''=2>0, so it is a global minimum (the function is convex), with value f(2)=3.

atoms.title: Multiple integrals and change of variables
atoms.summary: Integration extends to regions in many dimensions; changing coordinates rescales volume by the Jacobian determinant, the local volume-stretch factor of the transformation.

depths.eli5: To add up a quantity over a 2D or 3D region, slice it into tiny boxes and sum. If you switch to nicer coordinates (like polar), the tiny boxes change size, and the Jacobian is the bookkeeping factor that corrects for that stretching.
depths.core: Multiple integrals accumulate a function over a region, computed as iterated integrals (Fubini's theorem lets you integrate one variable at a time). Under a change of variables T, the volume element transforms by the absolute Jacobian determinant |det DT|, which is exactly the local volume-scaling of the map — connecting integration back to the determinant.
depths.deep: This is why polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates carry their characteristic factors (r, r, r²sin φ): each is a Jacobian. The same formula, read through differential forms, becomes orientation-aware and coordinate-free, feeding directly into the generalized Stokes' theorem and integration on manifolds.

atoms.note: The Jacobian is the multivariable derivative's determinant — it is the determinant atom doing the work of measuring how a coordinate change distorts volume.
atoms.art_prompt: a square grid in uv-coordinates warped into a curved grid in xy-coordinates, with one cell's area-change marked as the Jacobian

quiz.prompt: What factor appears when you change variables in a multiple integral, and what does it represent?
quiz.answer: The absolute value of the Jacobian determinant |det DT|; it represents the local factor by which the transformation stretches volume.

quiz.prompt: What is the area element dA in polar coordinates, and where does the extra factor come from?
quiz.answer: dA = r dr dθ; the factor r is the Jacobian determinant of the polar-to-Cartesian map, accounting for the larger area swept at larger radius.

atoms.title: Orthogonality and least squares
atoms.summary: Projecting onto a subspace gives the closest approximation; least squares solves overdetermined systems by orthogonally projecting the target onto the column space, leaving the smallest possible residual.

depths.eli5: If you can't hit a target exactly, aim for the closest reachable point — the one whose 'miss' is perpendicular to everything you can reach. That perpendicular drop is the best fit, and it's how you draw the best line through scattered data.
depths.core: Orthogonal projection of b onto a subspace is the unique closest point; the residual b − projection is orthogonal to the subspace. For an inconsistent system Ax=b, the least-squares solution minimizes ‖Ax−b‖ and is found by the normal equations AᵀAx̂=Aᵀb, geometrically projecting b onto the column space of A. Gram–Schmidt orthogonalizes a basis to make this clean.
depths.deep: Least squares is the linear-algebra core of regression, signal denoising, and data fitting; the orthogonality of the residual is precisely the first-order optimality condition. Numerically the normal equations square the condition number, so QR factorization or the SVD is preferred — the same projection, computed stably.

atoms.note: The defining feature of the best approximation is that the error vector is orthogonal to the subspace — minimizing distance and enforcing orthogonality are the same condition.
atoms.art_prompt: a point dropped perpendicularly onto a plane, the dashed projection meeting the plane at a right angle marking the closest point

quiz.prompt: What characterizes the least-squares solution geometrically?
quiz.answer: It is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A; the residual b − Ax̂ is perpendicular to that column space, making the error norm minimal.

quiz.prompt: Why do the normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb characterize the least-squares solution?
quiz.answer: Minimizing ‖Ax−b‖ requires the residual b−Ax̂ orthogonal to every column of A, i.e., Aᵀ(b−Ax̂)=0, which rearranges to AᵀAx̂=Aᵀb.

atoms.title: The singular value decomposition
atoms.summary: Every matrix factors into a rotation, a coordinate-aligned stretch, and another rotation; the singular values rank the directions of greatest action and yield the best low-rank approximation.

depths.eli5: Any linear transformation, no matter how messy, is secretly just: turn, stretch along clean axes, turn again. The stretch amounts (singular values) tell you which directions matter most — keep the biggest few and you get the best simple approximation of the whole thing.
depths.core: The SVD writes any m×n matrix as A=UΣVᵀ with U,V orthogonal and Σ diagonal of nonnegative singular values. The σᵢ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA, generalizing the spectral theorem to non-square, non-symmetric matrices. Truncating to the top k singular values gives the provably best rank-k approximation (Eckart–Young), the mathematical heart of dimensionality reduction.
depths.deep: The SVD unifies rank, range, null space, condition number, and pseudoinverse in one decomposition; it is the stable engine behind principal component analysis, latent semantic indexing, image compression, and recommendation systems. Geometrically it says every linear map maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid whose axes are the singular directions.

atoms.note: Singular values always exist and are real and nonnegative even when eigenvalues are complex or absent — the SVD is the more universal decomposition.
atoms.art_prompt: a unit circle mapped to an ellipse, the transformation broken into rotate, stretch along axes by sigma values, then rotate again

quiz.prompt: What does the singular value decomposition factor a matrix into, and how do singular values relate to eigenvalues?
quiz.answer: A = UΣVᵀ — an orthogonal rotation, a nonnegative diagonal stretch, and another orthogonal rotation; the singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA.

quiz.prompt: Explain why keeping the largest few singular values gives a good approximation of a matrix.
quiz.answer: By Eckart–Young, truncating to the top k singular values is the best possible rank-k approximation in norm. The largest σᵢ capture the directions where the matrix acts most strongly, so dropping the small ones discards the least information — the basis of PCA and compression.

atoms.title: Graphs and networks
atoms.summary: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges; this minimal structure models networks, and properties like connectivity, trees, and colorings turn relational questions into provable theorems.

depths.eli5: A graph is just dots connected by lines — friends and friendships, cities and roads, web pages and links. Even this bare picture has hard rules, like 'the total number of line-ends is always even.'
depths.core: A graph G=(V,E) abstracts pairwise relationships. The handshake lemma — the degrees sum to twice the edge count — is the first invariant. Trees (connected, acyclic) have exactly |V|−1 edges; paths, cycles, connectivity, bipartiteness, and planarity organize the theory. Euler's formula V−E+F=2 for planar graphs ties combinatorics to topology.
depths.deep: Graph theory is where many famous problems live: the four-color theorem, shortest paths (Dijkstra), spanning trees, and matchings. The graph Laplacian's spectrum (spectral graph theory) connects connectivity to eigenvalues, linking this discrete world back to linear algebra and to algorithms like PageRank and clustering.

atoms.note: The handshake lemma forces the number of odd-degree vertices to be even — a parity constraint that quietly settles many puzzles.
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: a network of labeled dots and connecting edges, one vertex's degree highlighted and a spanning tree drawn in bold

quiz.prompt: State the handshake lemma and one immediate consequence.
quiz.answer: The sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges; consequently the number of vertices of odd degree is always even.

quiz.prompt: How many edges does a tree with 10 vertices have?
quiz.answer: A tree on n vertices has exactly n−1 edges, so 10 vertices give 9 edges.

atoms.title: Recurrences and generating functions
atoms.summary: A recurrence defines each term from earlier ones; generating functions encode a whole sequence as a power series, converting recurrences into algebra and yielding closed forms.

depths.eli5: A recurrence is a rule like 'each number is the sum of the previous two' (Fibonacci). To find a formula instead of computing forever, you pack the whole sequence into a single power series and solve for it algebraically.
depths.core: Linear recurrences with constant coefficients solve via their characteristic equation — the same eigenvalue idea as for linear ODEs — giving closed forms as combinations of geometric terms. Generating functions Σaₙxⁿ turn the recurrence into an equation for the series; algebraic manipulation (partial fractions) then extracts the coefficients, e.g., Binet's formula for Fibonacci.
depths.deep: Generating functions are a dictionary between sequences and functions: convolution of sequences is multiplication of series, so counting problems with combinatorial structure become products. This analytic-combinatorics viewpoint, due to Euler and refined by Flajolet, extracts asymptotics of counts directly from the singularities of the generating function.

atoms.note: A linear recurrence is a linear map on the vector of recent terms — its long-term behavior is governed by the dominant eigenvalue (the golden ratio for Fibonacci).
sources: MIT OCW 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
atoms.art_prompt: a Fibonacci spiral beside a power series whose coefficients are the Fibonacci numbers being read off one at a time

quiz.prompt: How does a generating function help solve a recurrence?
quiz.answer: It encodes the whole sequence as a power series; the recurrence becomes an algebraic equation for that series, which you solve and then expand to read off a closed form for the terms.

quiz.prompt: What governs the growth rate of the Fibonacci numbers, and why?
quiz.answer: The golden ratio φ ≈ 1.618 — the dominant root of the characteristic equation x²=x+1; the largest-magnitude eigenvalue sets the long-term growth, so Fₙ grows like φⁿ.

atoms.title: Holomorphic functions and Cauchy's theorem
atoms.summary: Complex differentiability is so rigid that a once-differentiable function is infinitely differentiable and analytic; Cauchy's theorem makes contour integrals of such functions vanish, with values determined by boundary data.

depths.eli5: Being differentiable in the complex sense is a very strict demand — so strict that one derivative forces infinitely many, and the function is completely pinned down by its values on any loop around a point. Knowledge on the edge determines everything inside.
depths.core: A holomorphic function satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations and is automatically analytic (equal to its power series). Cauchy's integral theorem says the contour integral of a holomorphic function around a closed loop in a simply connected region is zero, and the integral formula reconstructs interior values from boundary values. Singularities are classified by their Laurent series, and the residue theorem evaluates integrals from them.
depths.deep: This rigidity has no real-variable analog and powers a remarkable toolkit: the residue theorem evaluates real definite integrals, analytic continuation extends functions uniquely (defining ζ(s) beyond its series), and Liouville's theorem yields the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. Complex analysis is where geometry, algebra, and analysis fuse most tightly.

atoms.note: Holomorphic equals analytic — a one-time complex derivative secretly guarantees infinite smoothness and a convergent power series, unlike the real case.
atoms.art_prompt: a closed contour in the complex plane encircling a point, arrows showing the integral of a holomorphic function summing to zero around it

quiz.prompt: What is surprising about complex differentiability compared to the real case?
quiz.answer: A single complex derivative forces the function to be infinitely differentiable and equal to its power series (holomorphic = analytic), whereas real differentiability does not even guarantee a second derivative.

quiz.prompt: Explain what Cauchy's integral formula says and why it is striking.
quiz.answer: It says a holomorphic function's value at an interior point equals a specific contour integral of the function around any loop enclosing it. Striking because the function's value inside is fully determined by its values on the boundary — interior behavior is dictated entirely by the edge.

atoms.title: Measure and the Lebesgue integral
atoms.summary: Measure theory assigns consistent sizes to sets and builds an integral by partitioning the range, not the domain — making limits and integration interchange and giving probability its rigorous foundation.

depths.eli5: Measure theory is the careful science of 'how big is this set?' — length, area, volume, probability, generalized. With it, you integrate by sorting outputs into bins instead of slicing inputs, which behaves far better when functions get wild.
depths.core: A measure μ assigns sizes to sets in a σ-algebra, satisfying countable additivity. The Lebesgue integral sums values weighted by the measure of the sets where they occur — partitioning the range rather than the domain — so it integrates functions Riemann cannot. Its convergence theorems (monotone, dominated) let you swap limits and integrals under mild hypotheses, the interchange real analysis needs.
depths.deep: Probability is exactly a measure of total mass 1, so random variables are measurable functions and expectation is a Lebesgue integral — measure theory is the rigorous language of probability. Not every set is measurable (the Banach–Tarski paradox exploits non-measurable sets via the axiom of choice), which is why σ-algebras restrict attention to the well-behaved ones.

atoms.note: Lebesgue partitions the range, Riemann the domain — that one switch is what makes badly discontinuous functions integrable and limit interchange safe.
atoms.art_prompt: a wild function shown sliced horizontally into range-bands, each band's preimage measured, contrasted with vertical Riemann slices

quiz.prompt: How does the Lebesgue integral differ in approach from the Riemann integral?
quiz.answer: Lebesgue partitions the range of the function and weights values by the measure of their preimages; Riemann partitions the domain into intervals. The Lebesgue approach integrates more functions and allows limit interchange.

quiz.prompt: Explain why measure theory is the natural foundation for probability.
quiz.answer: A probability is a measure with total mass 1; events are measurable sets, random variables are measurable functions, and expectation is the Lebesgue integral against the probability measure. Countable additivity gives exactly the axioms probability needs, so the whole theory is a special case of measure theory.

atoms.title: Manifolds and differential forms
atoms.summary: A manifold is a space that looks locally like flat Euclidean space; differential forms are the objects you integrate on it, and the exterior derivative generalizes grad, curl, and div at once.

depths.eli5: A manifold is a shape — a sphere, a torus, spacetime — that looks flat if you zoom in close enough, even though it curves globally. Differential forms are the things you can integrate over such shapes, and one operation generalizes all the calculus operators.
depths.core: An n-manifold is locally homeomorphic to ℝⁿ, stitched together by smooth coordinate charts. Calculus transfers via the tangent space at each point (a vector space of velocities) and differential forms, the objects integrated over submanifolds. The exterior derivative d unifies gradient, curl, and divergence; the identity d²=0 encodes that the boundary of a boundary is empty.
depths.deep: This is the language of modern geometry and physics: general relativity is the curvature of a Lorentzian manifold, gauge theory lives in fiber bundles over manifolds, and de Rham cohomology (closed forms modulo exact forms) detects a manifold's holes. The generalized Stokes' theorem ∫∂M ω = ∫M dω is the capstone, making integration intrinsically geometric.

atoms.note: The whole edifice is built so calculus is coordinate-free — forms and the exterior derivative transform correctly under any change of chart, unlike raw partial derivatives.
sources: MIT OCW 18.952 Theory of Differential Forms
atoms.art_prompt: a curved torus with a flat coordinate patch laid over a small region and a small oriented surface element carrying a differential form

quiz.prompt: What defines a manifold, and what role do differential forms play on it?
quiz.answer: A manifold looks locally like Euclidean space ℝⁿ via smooth coordinate charts; differential forms are the objects integrated over its submanifolds, with the exterior derivative generalizing grad, curl, and div.

quiz.prompt: Explain the meaning of the identity d²=0 and what it generalizes.
quiz.answer: Applying the exterior derivative twice always gives zero, mirroring that the boundary of a boundary is empty. It generalizes the vector-calculus identities curl(grad f)=0 and div(curl F)=0, and underlies de Rham cohomology and the generalized Stokes' theorem.
